papers.title: Scanning-probe quantum sensing of microwave and static magnetic field response of an on-chip superconducting resonator
papers.abstract: Superconducting resonators are finding increasing applications in designing advanced quantum circuits for ongoing sensing, metrology, and computing technological revolution. A detailed knowledge of microscopic electromagnetic properties of superconducting resonators is directly relevant for their further improvements on circuitry design and device performance. Here, we introduce scanning-probe quantum microscopy to report nanoscale sensing of microwave and static magnetic field environment of an on-chip niobium (Nb) superconducting resonator. Taking advantage of Rabi oscillation measurements, we show that microwave magnetic fields generated by the superconducting resonator mode can be utilized to achieve coherent control of a quantum spin sensor. We further visualize static electromagnetic field response of the Nb resonator, showing magnetic field-induced formation, evolution, and depinning of superconducting vortices. Our results provide insights into future design, testing and evaluation of solid-state superconducting resonators, highlighting the potential of quantum sensors as a local probe to investigate electromagnetic properties of superconducting quantum circuits.

summary.summary: Scanning-probe quantum microscopy using a quantum spin sensor locally probes the microwave and static magnetic field environment of an on-chip niobium superconducting resonator. Rabi oscillations enable coherent control of the spin sensor by the resonator's microwave mode, while static field measurements reveal vortex formation and depinning dynamics in the superconductor.
summary.motivation: Understanding microscopic electromagnetic properties of superconducting resonators is essential for optimizing their design and performance in quantum circuits, sensing, and metrology applications.
summary.method: A quantum spin sensor is scanned near an on-chip Nb resonator; Rabi oscillation measurements map the microwave magnetic field from the resonator mode, and static field response reveals vortex behavior under applied magnetic fields.
summary.result: The scanning-probe approach successfully achieves nanoscale spatial resolution of both the coherent microwave field distribution from the resonator and the static magnetic field-induced vortex dynamics in the Nb film.

papers.title: Profiling the Effective Limits of Error Mitigation via Circuit Replication
papers.abstract: Current era quantum computers continue to grow in both capability and capacity. Despite these advancements, errors induced by environmental noise severely limit practical applicability. Current research into error mitigation and correction to bridge the gap between current-era quantum computers and the execution of noise-sensitive workloads. These methods have significant performance and resource overheads, thereby greatly limiting the real-world benefits of their use. Circuit replication, as a naive form of error mitigation, is not new and has largely been ignored given the resource constraints of current quantum hardware. However, its simplicity is attractive as a means to supplement modern methods, reducing the overall performance overhead while still preserving error-mitigation capabilities. In this paper, we profile the effects of simple circuit replication under real-world noise profiles to better establish replication's limits as a supplemental mitigation strategy. Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for the Maxcut problem is explored for the analysis. For small graphs, we found that the average inference strength decreases by approximately 21.8% while the average standard deviation decreases by 108.8% compared to 6 replicates. For larger graphs, inference strength decreases by 35.4% while the average standard deviation decreased only 20.5%. Fewer replications did not affect smaller graphs, but degraded inference strength, with comparable benefits to standard deviation in larger graphs. These results show that replication has potential uses as a supplemental mitigation strategy for large-depth, highly variable workloads.

summary.summary: This paper characterizes circuit replication as a supplemental error mitigation strategy by executing QAOA for Maxcut on IBM's 156-qubit Fez platform with up to 6 parallel replicates on graphs with 5–8 nodes. For small graphs, 6 replicates reduce average standard deviation by 108.8% at the cost of 21.8% degradation in inference strength; for larger graphs, inference strength degrades 35.4% while standard deviation decreases only 20.5%, with variability plateauing between 3–4 replicates under the realistic noise model.
summary.motivation: NISQ devices suffer from high error rates and circuit depth constraints; while error correction techniques mitigate noise, they increase depth and resource overhead, motivating investigation of whether simple circuit replication can reduce output variability and serve as a lightweight supplement to more complex error mitigation schemes.
summary.method: Using Qiskit targeting IBM Fez connectivity, QAOA circuits for Maxcut were transpiled with a custom pass that duplicates programs stochastically via the transpiler to induce structural heterogeneity while preserving computational homogeneity, simulated under both noiseless and realistic hardware noise models for replication levels 1–6, and analyzed using inference strength (ratio of successful trial frequency to highest erroneous trial frequency) and standard deviation across ten trials per configuration.
summary.result: Replication stabilizes output variability without improving average inference strength—6 replicates reduce standard deviation by up to 108.8% for small graphs but degrade inference strength by 21.8%–35.4% due to accumulated gate errors, with diminishing returns after 3–4 replicates in noisy simulation, suggesting utility only for large-depth variability-sensitive workloads rather than as a standalone mitigation strategy.
